effect_estimate.comment: No primary statistical effect estimate is computed; secondary descriptive policy figures (<0.01% of Australian water diversions; up to 25% draft Indigenous reserve in Mataranka) are reported alongside qualitative comparative institutional findings.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Statutory water modernisation reforms in Australia (vesting water in the Crown, unbundling tradeable private water entitlements from land title, restricting Native Title water rights to non-commercial domestic/subsistence uses, and relying on non-mandatory planning provisions) and emerging state water reforms in East Timor (state ownership, proposed cost-recovery tariffs, and subordinating customary governance/tara bandu to statutory law) marginalise or only superficially engage customary water governance and fail to prioritise Indigenous water allocations; in Australia, Indigenous-specific water entitlements account for less than 0.01% of total water diversions (citing Jackson & Langton, 2012), although a draft Northern Territory plan (Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan) proposes allocating up to 25% of the consumptive pool to Indigenous landowners.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 10-12, Statutory Systems in Australia & Community Strategies; PDF pp. 13-16, Statutory Systems in East Timor & Community Strategies; PDF pp. 16-18, Discussion

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework design ceiling. Rated 2 because the study directly documents concrete statutory, judicial, planning, and state-customary institutional mechanisms (conversion of licences into unbundled private water entitlements, subsistence-only Native Title interpretations, non-mandatory water planning participation, proposed cost-recovery tariffs, and selective state co-optation of tara bandu ceremonies) operating on Indigenous and local water access and governance.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 9-12, Statutory Systems in Australia; PDF pp. 13-16, Statutory Systems in East Timor; PDF pp. 16-18, Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines statutory property and social/native title tenure regimes (property, tenure), catchment/aquifer water allocation planning (planning), consumption pricing, user fees, and proposed state cost-recovery tariffs (fees), recognition/accommodation of customary water governance and Indigenous cultural reserves (accommodation), Indigenous and community participation in water planning and supply management (participation), customary and state-backed enforcement sanctions (sanction), and High Court jurisprudence / statutory court review provisions (judicial_review).

sample_size.comment: The paper presents a qualitative comparative legal-institutional analysis of two national case studies (Australia and East Timor) drawing on legislation, policy documents, secondary literature, and prior fieldwork, without reporting a primary sample size of interviews, households, or observations.
